title: Can Educational Equality Be Engineered through Competition
author: Samuel Kammin
summary: Samuel Kammin writes up his visit to St Thomas the Apostle College in Nunhead, London, a Catholic boys' comprehensive that moved from the bottom of the Southwark league tables to an Outstanding Ofsted rating and a Progress 8 score of +1.45. He frames the visit with the old argument between meritocracy and egalitarianism and asks whether a strict, no excuses school can engineer equality of opportunity. The school's system rests on termly assessment, phones collected at the gate, a merit and demerit point system, streaming by ability, and a rank order of pupils displayed publicly on noticeboards. Leaders defend the ranking as transparent for parents and as healthy preparation for the world of work, and they reject the language of disadvantage as an excuse. Kammin weighs this against research on the Big-Fish-Little-Pond effect and on competition reducing cooperation, and he notes that pastoral meetings precede publication and that some pupils are exempted. He closes by suggesting that high expectations and care need not be opposites, while admitting that measurement alone cannot settle whether inequality is overcome.
points: St Thomas the Apostle's turnaround is credited by its leaders to structure, discipline and a refusal to patronise pupils, including the 50 percent eligible for free school meals.
The public rank order, built from academic results plus behaviour and effort, is defended as a transparent signal to parents and a motivator, though it guarantees someone is always at the bottom.
Research cited by the author is mixed: rank can shape academic self-concept and subject choice, and explicit competition can reduce willingness to help peers and even effort among high achievers.
The school pairs its no excuses stance with pastoral safeguards, such as meetings with vulnerable pupils before rankings go up and exemptions during bereavement or illness.
Pupils quoted describe strictness as a sign that teachers are invested in their futures, which challenges the assumption that care and uncompromising expectations conflict.
quotes: In large part, the current and most vocal attitude of many schools in England is in keeping with the meritocratic view; that education should enable hardworking and talented students to succeed regardless of their circumstances.

Despite the school’s high level of socioeconomic challenges (over 50% qualify for free school meals), the leadership team refuse to call their pupils ‘disadvantaged,’ arguing that the ‘disadvantage’ label allows excuses to weasel through.
On entry to the school premises each morning, all phones are collected in a bag by staff as children arrange themselves in lines before they enter their classrooms for registration.

The rank order system is a public display of children’s rank relative to their peers. Each child’s position is calculated by using their average academic performance across their full range of subjects, as well as their overall behaviour and effort track, which is displayed around the premises for the whole school to see.

More troublingly, there is a legitimate concern that when academic success becomes explicitly competitive, children may be less willing to help one another, turning potential collaborators into rivals.
By its nature, this will inevitably mean there is always a child at the bottom, but the school argued that this is a part of the healthy competitive game and a reality of the world of work.
It’s not anti woke, it’s pro kid. Expectation levels are everything.” - Executive Headteacher
Indeed, being held to demanding standards can itself be experienced as a sign that adults believe in your potential just as much as any child.
